cards.front: Qualified account
cards.back: A retirement account that qualifies for tax-deferred growth. Some require employer sponsorship; others (like IRAs) do not. Technically, IRAs are not 'qualified plans' under the IRS, but they share most of the same rules.

cards.front: What type of income must be used to fund IRA contributions?
cards.back: Earned income only (salary, wages, tips, commissions). Ordinary income items such as dividends, interest, and capital gains do not qualify.

cards.front: Is there an age limit for making contributions to a traditional or Roth IRA?
cards.back: No. There is no age limit for IRA contributions, but the contributor must have earned income.

cards.front: By what date must IRA contributions for a given tax year be made?
cards.back: By the first tax filing deadline of the following year (normally April 15). No extensions.

cards.front: What is the catch-up contribution amount for IRA owners age 50 or older?
cards.back: An additional $1,000 above the normal annual contribution limit.

cards.front: Which investments are NOT permitted inside an IRA?
cards.back: Collectibles (antiques, gems, rare coins, art, stamps) and life insurance contracts. (U.S.-minted gold and silver coins ARE permitted.)

cards.front: Which investment practices are considered inappropriate for IRAs and other retirement plans?
cards.back: Short selling stock, speculative option strategies, buying tax-exempt municipal securities, and margin trading. Covered call writing IS permitted (conservative income generation).

cards.front: IRA rollover
cards.back: When a customer withdraws and takes possession of IRA assets and returns them to an IRA (or other qualified account) within 60 calendar days. Limited to one rollover per rolling 12-month period per person (not per account).

cards.front: How does an IRA transfer (custodian-to-custodian) differ from a rollover?
cards.back: In a transfer, assets move directly between custodians and the owner never takes possession. There is no limit on the number of transfers per year, and no 60-day rule applies. A move from a 401(k) to an IRA is technically a transfer (sometimes called a 'direct rollover').

cards.front: What is the tax treatment of withdrawals from a traditional IRA before age 59½?
cards.back: Taxed as ordinary income PLUS a 10% premature distribution penalty, unless an exception applies.

cards.front: List the exceptions allowing penalty-free traditional IRA withdrawals before age 59½.
cards.back: Death of the owner; disability of the owner; first-time home purchase (up to $10,000); qualified education expenses (taxpayer, spouse, child, or grandchild); medical insurance premiums for the unemployed; medical expenses exceeding defined AGI limits.

cards.front: When must required minimum distributions (RMDs) begin from a traditional IRA?
cards.back: Beginning in the year the owner turns 72, and annually by December 31 thereafter. The first RMD may be delayed until April 1 of the following year, but then a second RMD must also be taken by December 31 of that same year.

cards.front: What is the penalty for failing to take a required minimum distribution (RMD) from a traditional IRA?
cards.back: 50% of the difference between the required amount and the amount actually withdrawn.

cards.front: An investor age 75 has three traditional IRAs at a bank, an insurance company, and a broker-dealer. The combined RMD is $20,000. How may the investor satisfy the RMD?
cards.back: The full $20,000 can be taken from any one account or split in any combination among the three accounts, as long as the total withdrawn equals $20,000.

cards.front: Are contributions to a Roth IRA tax-deductible?
cards.back: No. Roth contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are NOT deductible from current income. However, qualified distributions (including growth) are tax-free.

cards.front: If the annual IRA contribution limit is $6,000, can an investor contribute $6,000 to a traditional IRA AND $6,000 to a Roth IRA in the same year?
cards.back: No. The limit is a combined limit across all IRAs. The investor could split the $6,000 in any combination (e.g., $4,000 traditional + $2,000 Roth).

cards.front: What two conditions must be met for a Roth IRA distribution to be 'qualified' (tax-free)?
cards.back: (1) The account must have been held for at least 5 years, AND (2) the owner must be at least 59½. Exceptions to the age requirement: death, disability, or first-time home purchase (up to $10,000).

cards.front: How are nonqualified distributions of earnings from a Roth IRA taxed?
cards.back: Taxed as ordinary income AND subject to a 10% premature distribution penalty. Distributions of cost basis (contributions) are always tax-free.

cards.front: Do Roth IRAs have required minimum distributions (RMDs)?
cards.back: No. Roth IRAs have no RMD requirement. The owner may leave the funds in the account for life.

cards.front: What is the penalty for making an excess contribution to an IRA?
cards.back: A 6% penalty assessed on the excess contribution amount every year until it is withdrawn.

cards.front: Chris, age 60, opened a Roth IRA 10 years ago contributing $3,000/year. The account is now worth $60,000. He withdraws $5,000. What is the tax treatment?
cards.back: No tax is owed. Chris is over 59½ and has held the Roth more than 5 years, so the distribution is qualified and entirely tax-free.

cards.front: Defined benefit plan
cards.back: A qualified employer-sponsored retirement plan (traditional pension) that defines the retirement benefit the employee will receive, typically based on years of service, age, and salary. The employer bears the investment risk and must fund the plan to meet promised benefits.

cards.front: Defined contribution plan
cards.back: A qualified employer-sponsored plan that defines the amount that may be contributed each year. Employees direct the investments and bear the investment risk. The retirement benefit depends on contributions and investment performance. Examples: 401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, money purchase, SIMPLE plans.

cards.front: In a defined benefit plan vs. a defined contribution plan, who bears the investment risk?
cards.back: Defined benefit: the employer bears the investment risk (must fund the promised benefit). Defined contribution: the employee bears the investment risk.

cards.front: Joe retires at age 65 after 40 years at Rick & Ty's Furniture. The plan pays 2% per year of service × average salary of last 5 years, capped at 70%. His 5-year average salary is $60,000. What is his annual pension?
cards.back: 40 × 2% = 80%, which exceeds the 70% cap, so 70% applies. 70% × $60,000 = $42,000 per year for life.

cards.front: Why are defined contribution plans more popular today than traditional pensions?
cards.back: The investment risk shifts from employer to employee (lower employer liability), and assets are portable between employer plans, which benefits a mobile workforce.

cards.front: What risk does a retiree from a private-sector defined benefit pension typically bear?
cards.back: Purchasing power (inflation) risk — the fixed monthly benefit does not adjust for inflation. Government pensions often include a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA).
